source.title: Assessing the quality of the datasets by identifying mislabeled samples
source.authors: Vaibhav Pulastya; Gaurav Nuti; Yash Kumar Atri; Tanmoy Chakraborty

record.tranche_reason: Tests classification performance after adding random or systematic label corruption to image datasets, a related noisy-label setting. It does not reproduce the random-label fitting experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper reports clean-test classification accuracy for standard training on corrupted datasets and for several filtering methods. Only standard-training results bear on the claim versions here. Mislabel-identification scores and results for AQUAVS, LabelFix, Entropy TD, and Oracle are not rows because they evaluate filtering or alternative methods, not the claimed standard-network behavior. Training error is not reported.
record.test_reason: The standard-training results under uniform random label corruption test V4's test-performance component in additional datasets and architectures. They do not establish perfect fitting or memorization of corrupted training labels.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that AQUAVS noise scores identify mislabeled samples and that filtering improves clean-test classification performance over standard training, with only slight improvements on CIFAR100. Their explanation that networks learn label noise is not backed here by reported training-error measurements.
record.recipe_differences: Uses supervised variational-autoencoder latent representations to identify mislabeled samples, then trains classifiers on filtered data. It does not use the original random-label fitting intervention or its training-error measure.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset, noise type, and corruption rate; systematic noise is described as harder to filter than uniform noise, and the CIFAR100 high-noise setting as particularly challenging.

fits_no_version.finding: Under systematic corruption, selected examples from class l receive label (l+1) modulo the number of classes. Test accuracy generally decreases, with a small MNIST increase between 20% and 30% corruption.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing systematic class-dependent label corruption generally reduces clean-test accuracy under standard training.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Advances in Social Networks Analysis and Mining
record.problems: The paper reports clean-test accuracy but not training error on corrupted labels, so it cannot establish whether standard training fits those labels. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The standard MNIST results use a 5% subsample of the training set.
record.rows_left_out: Rows for AQUAVS, LabelFix, Entropy TD, and Oracle in Tables IV–V were left out because they concern filtering methods or the oracle comparator, not standard-network results. Mislabel-identification metrics in Tables II–III do not measure the claim versions.

untested.parts: Complete random labeling, zero or near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged training hyperparameters.
Relative training time and convergence speed as corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.

Perfect fitting of corrupted training sets, direct evidence of memorizing noise, the uncorrupted baseline, corruption above 40% through complete random labeling, and the chance endpoint. Sparse corruption levels do not establish smoothness between measurements.
Effects of adding or removing weight decay, dropout, and data augmentation.
The temporal order of learning real-label patterns and memorizing noise.

record.verdict_notes: All extracted numerical values and model assignments match Tables IV–V and Section V.C. Observed states for uniform-noise rows refer only to the measured test-performance trend. Missing training-error measurements are untested components, not evidence of incomplete fitting. Systematic-noise results are kept separate because their incorrect labels are fixed by class rather than randomly assigned. No uncertainty estimates support interpreting the small systematic-noise MNIST fluctuation as a reliable reversal.

versions.untested_parts: Does not report training error on completely random labels or test error at chance.
Does not compare training time or convergence speed for true versus random labels.
Does not test shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

Reports test accuracy under several label-corruption rates, but does not report whether the standard models fit the corrupted training sets perfectly. The tested rates stop at 40%, not all corruption levels through 100%.
Does not test weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation as factors in fitting random labels or generalizing on true labels.
Does not measure the order in which real-label patterns and noise are learned over training.

relationships.condition: Standard training with uniform random label corruption at the reported rates
relationships.reason: Test accuracy decreases monotonically: MNIST 94.3→90.3%, FashionMNIST 89.5→86.5%, CIFAR10 72.6→57.5%, and CIFAR100 47.7→39.7% (R1–R4, R9–R12, R17–R18, R21–R22). This supports only V4's test-degradation component.
relationships.display_finding: Test accuracy fell monotonically from 94.3% to 90.3% on MNIST, 89.5% to 86.5% on FashionMNIST, 72.6% to 57.5% on CIFAR10, and 47.7% to 39.7% on CIFAR100.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Standard training on MNIST, FashionMNIST, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100 at the reported corruption rates
reader_labels.reason: Clean-test accuracy generally falls as corruption increases, consistent with degradation in test performance (R1–R24). The study does not report training error, so this supports only the test-performance portion.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Systematic noise on MNIST at 20% and 30% corruption
reader_labels.reason: Accuracy rises from 91.2 to 91.7 rather than degrading steadily across these reported rates (R6–R7).
